entries.title: How a magnetic compass points a direction
entries.answer: A compass has a magnetic needle that can turn with little friction. Earth has a magnetic field that gives the needle a direction. The end marked north generally points close to geographic north in many places, but the exact direction depends on where you stand. Maps can give a correction for this difference. A magnet or a piece of iron held nearby can also pull the needle away from where it would otherwise point.
facts: The angle between local compass north and geographic north is called magnetic declination.

entries.title: How can a printer use the same letters in different books?
entries.answer: Movable type uses small pieces with letters or other signs on their faces. A printer sets the pieces in a frame to make lines of writing, puts ink on them, and presses them against paper. After making enough copies, the printer can take the pieces apart and arrange them to make another page. In Europe, Gutenberg’s workshop used a system like this in the 1400s. People in East Asia had made books with movable type earlier.
facts: The Gutenberg Bible was printed in Europe around 1455.

entries.title: How did people turn plant material into paper?
entries.answer: To make many kinds of paper, people separate plant material into tiny strands, mix them with water, and lift a thin layer on a screen. As the water drains, the strands stay in a mat. Pressing and drying make the mat into a sheet. People in China used paper early in its history, and workshops improved ways of making it over time. The idea of making light sheets from wet strands gave writers another choice besides heavier surfaces such as stone or clay.
facts: Archaeological finds show that some paper existed in China before the official Cai Lun reported improvements in 105 CE.

entries.title: How quartz helps a clock count seconds
entries.answer: A quartz clock contains a little piece of a mineral that can vibrate. An electronic circuit gives the quartz small pushes so it vibrates at a regular rate. The clock counts those vibrations and turns each set into a step of time. That step can update a display or tell a tiny motor to move hands. Older mechanical clocks can count swings of a much bigger part. The quartz clock uses a much smaller movement.
facts: A common watch crystal vibrates more than thirty thousand times in one second.

entries.title: How the Wright brothers learned to fly
entries.answer: Orville and Wilbur Wright tested gliders to learn how to balance an aircraft and turn it. They also made a wind tunnel to try different wing shapes before they built their powered Flyer. In December 1903, near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, Orville flew it first. The brothers took turns through four flights that day. Being able to steer mattered as much as being able to lift off, since an airplane has to stay under control in moving air.
facts: The Wright brothers had worked repairing and making bicycles in Dayton, Ohio.

entries.title: What do the stripes on a barcode say?
entries.answer: A striped barcode uses dark bars and light gaps of different widths to represent numbers. A scanner can shine light on the stripes and measure the pattern that comes back. The equipment turns that pattern into a number with a known meaning. At a store, the number often identifies the type and size of product so a computer can look up its name or its price. Bottles of the same kind can share the same number.
facts: A store’s own computer normally looks up the price. The stripes do not need to spell out a dollar amount.
